title: Can two by one tiles cover a four by seven grid?
description: A grid of four rows and seven columns. The squares count to an even number, and every column holds four squares, so two upright tiles fill each column. Keeko's doubt, that an odd number of columns spoils it, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: look at the length of one column, not the number of columns. Watch for students who think an odd number of columns stops a tiling.

source: Can a 4 × 7 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
video_script.why: The child sees that a grid with an odd number of columns can still be tiled when each column has an even length.
video_script.substitution: Each column has four squares, so two vertical tiles fill it, whatever the number of columns.
video_script.anchor: A grid of unit squares with 4 rows and 7 columns, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks an odd number of columns means the grid can never be tiled. But each column has four squares, so two tiles fill it, and seven columns can be filled one by one.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, the grid can be tiled with fourteen vertical tiles, two in each column.

final_answer.value: Yes: 14 vertical tiles, 2 in each column
final_answer.spoken: yes, fourteen vertical tiles, two in each column

maths_rules: The grid has 4 × 7 = 28 unit squares, an even number, so 14 tiles would be needed.
Each of the 7 columns has 4 squares.
Two vertical tiles cover each column.
7 columns use 7 × 2 = 14 tiles, with no gap and no overlap.
Slip: an odd number of columns does not stop a tiling; the length of one column matters.
video_script.design: One grid, one tile. The squares are counted, then the columns are filled in turn. The slip is blaming the odd number of columns.
